claims.claim: Sampling is the selection of a subset of a population to estimate characteristics of the whole population.
The population is the complete group a question is about; the sample is the subset actually examined.
Researchers use samples because studying an entire population often costs too much or is virtually impossible.
In random sampling, every member of the population has a chance of being selected; in a simple random sample, members initially have an equal chance.
Stratified sampling divides the population into groups called strata and takes a proportionate random sample from each group.
Sampling bias occurs when a sample is collected so that some members of the population are more likely to be included than others, making the sample unrepresentative and its results inaccurate.
Larger samples tend to be more reliable than smaller ones, but a biased sample that does not represent the population gives inaccurate results even when it is large.
Sample-based estimates come with uncertainty, reported as a margin of error: a range around the estimate within which the true population value is likely to fall.
The U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey samples about 3.5 million addresses per year rather than attempting a full count of the population.
The Census Bureau selects a random sample of addresses for the ACS; each address has about a 1-in-480 chance of being selected in a given month and is not selected more than once every five years.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does a larger sample always give better results?
positions: OpenStax Introductory Statistics: "Larger samples are better, if possible," because samples that are too small may be unreliable.

The same source states that biased samples that are not representative of the population give results that are inaccurate and not valid, and convenience samples can be highly biased regardless of how many people are included.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both principles together: larger samples tend to reduce random variation, but size cannot repair bias. Representation is what makes a sample a valid stand-in for the population, so the two positions are consistent once bias is separated from random variation.
